newsitem.title: UK: Budget won't blow stg off bullish course - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Budget won't blow stg off bullish course - analysts.

text.p: Sterling seesawed its way through a complex UK 1997/8 budget, but on balance the package contained little to blow it off its current bullish course, analysts said.

The pound stood near 2.5528 marks when Chancellor Kenneth Clarke began his budget speech, sprinted to a 32-month high of 2.5586 when public borrowing forecasts were cut, but then retreated after Clarke cast doubt on future interest rate rises.
Analysts said the case for monetary tightening, a key factor in sterling's recent appreciation, remained intact and should keep the pound in fine fettle.

"I don't see the reasons for the pound's rise being changed at the moment," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered in London. "It doesnt remove the possibility of interest rate rises earlier rather than later."
The public sector borrowing requirement forecast for 1997/8 was lowered to 19.0 billion stg from the previous forecast of 23.0 billion and to 26.5 billion in 1996/7 from 27 billion.

While Clarke cut one point off basic income tax, he raised a number of indirect taxes, scrapped several tax breaks, and said the UK current account would remain broadly in balance this year and next. All these were sterling-positive, analysts said.

"The market can expect interest rates to move in a different direction to its European neighbours," said Stephen Hannah, director of research at IBJ International in London. "Sterling will maintain its upward trend in the near term."
But Clarke moved to quell some market rate-hike optimism.

"I am tightening fiscal policy now to reduce the risk of having to tighten monetary policy excessively as I set policy to hit my inflation target," Clarke told parliament, saying he aimed to get underlying inflation down to 2.5 percent or less.
That was a signal Clarke would become more resistant to Bank of England calls for more tightening, analysts warned.
"(The budget) doesn't reduce the case for an interest rate rise, but it marginally reduces the prospect of an interest rate rise," said Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel here.
The market was caught unawares by a quarter-point UK base rate increase on October 30, and a welter of buoyant economic data since then has nourished market rate-hike speculation.

Cole felt the overall currency impact of the budget was broadly neutral. But the diminished prospect of a rate hike, combined with market concern over whether the government indeed had the revenue measures to offset its tax cuts, could swing the implications for sterling narrowly into negative, he said.
Sterling was trading at 2.5515/25 marks and $1.6720/25 at 1800 GMT compared to 2.5528/39 and 1.6687/97 when Clarke began to unveil his budget, the last before the general election.
It ended European dealings at around 2.5403/14 marks and $1.6722/32 on Monday.

Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch, said sterling's strength -- which has taken it recently to four-year highs against the dollar -- should continue, possibly despite rather than because of the 1997/8 budget.
"I think generally the pound will remain quite strong but it has little to do with this budget," Prendergast said.
"If anything, the combination of tight fiscal and loose monetary policy would be negative but I think we're pretty well underpinned on other factors and the budget will have little net impact".
